title: Kubernetes Pod
content: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage volumes. Pods are ephemeral: when one dies, a controller creates a replacement with a new IP address.

title: Kubernetes Deployment
content: A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet and declares the desired number of identical Pods. It performs rolling updates by default, replacing Pods gradually so the service stays available, and it can roll back to a previous revision.

title: Kubernetes Service
content: A Service gives a set of Pods a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances traffic across them. ClusterIP is the default type and is reachable only inside the cluster.

title: Kubernetes Probes
content: Liveness probes restart a container that is stuck. Readiness probes remove a Pod from Service endpoints until it can handle traffic. Startup probes give slow-starting containers time to boot before the other probes begin.

title: Resource Requests and Limits
content: Requests are what the scheduler reserves for a container, and limits are the maximum it may use. CPU above the limit is throttled, and a container that exceeds its memory limit is killed with OOMKilled. Utilization-based autoscaling is computed against requests.

title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
content: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts a Deployment's replica count based on observed metrics, most commonly average CPU utilization compared with the requested CPU. It needs a metrics source such as metrics-server and respects minReplicas and maxReplicas.

title: ConfigMap and Secret
content: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration and Secrets hold sensitive values such as passwords and API keys. Both can be injected as environment variables or mounted as files. Secrets are only base64 encoded by default, so they should not be committed to Git in plain form.

title: Kubernetes StatefulSet
content: A StatefulSet manages Pods that need stable network identities and persistent storage, such as databases. Each Pod gets a stable name and its own PersistentVolumeClaim that survives rescheduling.

title: Kubernetes Namespace
content: Namespaces divide a cluster into virtual sections for names, access control, and resource quotas. They are commonly used to separate teams, environments, or system components such as monitoring.

title: kind
content: kind runs Kubernetes clusters using Docker containers as nodes. It is designed for local development and CI testing. Images built locally must be loaded into the cluster, or pulled from a registry.

title: GitOps
content: GitOps keeps the desired state of a system in Git and uses an automated agent to make the live system match it. Changes happen through commits and reviews rather than manual kubectl commands, which gives an audit trail and easy rollbacks.

title: Argo CD Application
content: An Argo CD Application ties a Git path or Helm chart to a destination cluster and namespace. Argo CD compares the live state with the desired state, reports whether the app is Synced and Healthy, and can apply changes automatically.

title: Argo CD Sync Policy
content: With automated sync, Argo CD applies changes from Git without a manual step. Prune deletes resources that were removed from Git, and selfHeal reverts manual changes made directly in the cluster so the live state matches Git again.

title: App of Apps Pattern
content: The app-of-apps pattern uses one root Argo CD Application whose source contains other Application manifests. Applying the single root bootstraps the whole platform, and sync waves control the order in which child applications are created.

title: Prometheus Scraping
content: Prometheus pulls metrics over HTTP from targets at a regular scrape interval, usually from a /metrics endpoint. Each time series is identified by a metric name and labels. Pull-based collection makes it easy to see which targets are down.

title: Prometheus Metric Types
content: A counter only increases and is used for totals such as requests or tokens. A gauge can go up and down, such as memory in use. A histogram counts observations into buckets, which lets PromQL estimate percentiles of values like request latency.

title: PromQL Latency Percentile
content: To estimate p95 latency from a histogram, use histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(metric_bucket[5m]))). The rate function turns cumulative bucket counters into per-second rates over a window, and the le label is the bucket boundary.

title: ServiceMonitor
content: A ServiceMonitor is a custom resource from the Prometheus Operator that tells Prometheus which Services to scrape, on which port and path. It lets teams declare scraping next to their application manifests instead of editing Prometheus configuration.

title: Prometheus Alerting Rules
content: A Prometheus alerting rule fires when its PromQL expression is true for the duration set by the for field, which avoids alerting on brief spikes. With the Prometheus Operator, rules are declared using a PrometheusRule resource.

title: Grafana Dashboards
content: Grafana visualizes data from sources such as Prometheus using panels organized into dashboards. Dashboards can be stored as JSON and provisioned automatically, for example from ConfigMaps picked up by a sidecar, so they live in Git.

title: pgvector
content: pgvector adds a vector column type and similarity operators to PostgreSQL. The <=> operator returns cosine distance, where smaller means more similar. An HNSW index speeds up nearest neighbor search at the cost of approximate results.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
content: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant documents for a question and gives them to a language model as context, so the answer is grounded in known sources instead of the model's memory. Quality depends on both retrieval and how closely the model sticks to the context.

title: LangGraph
content: LangGraph models an agent workflow as a graph of nodes that read and update a shared state, connected by edges. Conditional edges let the workflow branch, for example skipping generation when retrieval finds nothing.

title: Latency Percentiles
content: p50 is the median request time, while p95 is the time under which 95 percent of requests finish. Tail percentiles such as p95 expose slow outliers that averages hide, so they are the usual basis for latency alerts and service level objectives.
